When something ricochets, it hits a hard surface and bounces off in a new direction, continuing to move rather than stopping. Think of throwing a stone at a wall — if it hits the wall and shoots off sideways instead of falling straight down, that's a ricochet. The object arrives from one direction, makes contact with a surface, and leaves in a different direction.
What makes it different from simply "bouncing"

This is where the sharpness of the word lives. "Bounce" is broad and neutral — a basketball bouncing on a court is calm, expected, and controlled. Ricochet is different in feel. It almost always implies speed, force, and a sense of the object going somewhere unintended or uncontrolled. When something ricochets, there is an energy to it — the surface couldn't fully absorb the impact, so the object is violently redirected. This is why the word is most naturally used for bullets, stones, balls, and sound — fast, hard things hitting hard surfaces.

A bullet fired at a metal wall does not bounce. It ricochets — shooting off at an angle, carrying its full dangerous energy in a new, unpredictable direction. That sense of danger, speed, and unpredictability is baked into the word.

The most classic use is with bullets. A bullet can ricochet off a wall, a rock, or the ground, meaning it deflects sharply off the surface and flies in a new direction. This is why in action movies, you'll often hear the sharp whizzing sound of a bullet that hit a surface and went somewhere unintended.

Stones do it too. When children skip stones across a lake, each time the stone glances off the water's surface and jumps forward again, it is technically ricocheting — the stone hits, doesn't sink, and keeps going.

Balls in sports ricochet off posts, boards, and walls. In soccer, a ball can ricochet off the goalpost. In billiards (pool), ricocheting off the cushions is the whole game, though players there usually say "bank" or "rebound."

Sound can also ricochet. In a large empty hall or a cave, sound waves hit the hard walls and ricochet back to you, which is how echoes work.
How to use it in a sentence

The most natural structure is: something ricochets off a surface.

The bullet ricocheted off the concrete floor.
The ball ricocheted off the post and went out of bounds.
Her voice ricocheted off the walls of the empty warehouse.

You can also say something ricochets around a space, meaning it bounces off multiple surfaces within it.

The sound of the gunshot ricocheted around the canyon.

Or from one thing to another:

The puck ricocheted from the boards to the stick.
Figurative uses — and this is important

Ricochet is also used figuratively, and this is where the word becomes truly powerful in writing and speech. When effects, consequences, or feelings spread outward from a single source — especially in unexpected or uncontrolled ways — writers use ricochet to describe it.

The scandal ricocheted through the company, leaving no department untouched.
The economic crash of that year ricocheted across the world.
The news ricocheted around the internet within minutes.
The pain of his words ricocheted inside her long after he'd left.

In every figurative case, the logic is the same as the literal one: something hits a point of impact, and instead of stopping there, it bounces outward — spreading, affecting other things, going further than expected, and often in directions that are hard to predict or control. The figurative use keeps that sense of uncontrolled, energetic spreading.

If you had to feel the personality of ricochet, it is a word of speed, sharp angles, hard surfaces, and lack of control. It is never a gentle word. Nothing ever ricochets softly. The word itself sounds like what it describes — sharp, quick, with a snap to it. Use it when you want to convey that something fast and forceful hit something solid and was sent flying in an unintended direction, whether that's a bullet off a wall or bad news through a crowd.
